title: Wolff reflects on impact of tow in Las Vegas Qualifying
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained how Mercedes learned about the effectiveness of the slipstream during Qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Silver Arrows Team Principal believing George Russell had been ideally positioned to secure pole.

Mercedes enjoyed a strong session as Kimi Antonelli topped the timesheets ahead of Max Verstappen and Russell, but a five-place grid penalty for the Italian due to power unit changes means he will start sixth, promoting his team mate to the front row alongside the Dutchman.

The final stages of Qualifying saw drivers jostling for position to benefit from a tow along the circuit's lengthy straights, something Wolff explained had caught Mercedes by surprise.

"I've had 35 years in motorsport," Wolff told F1 TV. "I've never seen tows working when you're one and a half seconds behind each other like a train, because normally you should be penalised through the corners so much that the straights never compensate for it.

"But for whatever reason, here it seems to work. We found out later than some of the other teams, and I have no idea how these lap times came together."

Antonelli made the decision himself to drop to the back of the queue ahead of his final flying lap, with Mercedes initially concerned he wouldn't reach the line with enough time to start.

"We thought he wouldn't cross the line in time," Wolff explained. "But the truth is, even if he had, he would have been much too close to the car ahead of him, and so that lap for me was gone. And then, for whatever miracle reason, it was fast."

Speaking separately to Sky Sports F1, Wolff explained that he had expected Russell to be in contention for pole, although Mercedes still needed to investigate where the Briton had lost time.

"George, for me, had the perfect position. He was four seconds behind the car in front," Wolff said.

"We need to find out because I think there was something in Turns 7, 8 and 9, whether that was a mistake or something else happened. But it looked like the ideal position for a pole lap because he was quickest all the time."

Looking ahead to Russell starting alongside Verstappen, Wolff added: "Big cinema if they try to go through the first corners together. We shall be watching."

title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Las Vegas GP?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli was quickest in Qualifying but a five-place grid drop means Max Verstappen inherited pole position in Las Vegas, but will he be able to convert that to victory on Saturday night?

Running in FP3 – our only dry practice session – suggested Red Bull and McLaren, while substantially quicker than Mercedes through the twisty middle sector, are losing almost a second to the Silver Arrows on the straights. The tow hid that in Qualifying, but in the race, it’s the sort of deficit that can shake-out an order pretty quickly.

That is, of course, if the race goes by the numbers – and frankly, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit just isn’t that sort of track. While offering ample overtaking opportunities, it is also capricious: low-grip, omnipresent walls, and perfectly able to supply a game-changing Safety Car, VSC or red flag. Taking the jackpot in Vegas requires a quick car and a solid plan. The quick car alone won’t be good enough.

title: What To Watch For in the Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
From an eye-catching front row to Ferrari trying to recover from Qualifying disappointment, and from drivers starting out of position due to grid penalties to a forecast for one of the coldest races in history, here are five things to keep an eye on ahead of a spectacular evening under the lights in Las Vegas…

1. Verstappen vs Russell

Robust racing had broken out between Max Verstappen and George Russell even before we reached a competitive session this weekend, as an incident in FP3 led to the pair having to visit the stewards.

Verstappen overtook Russell before Turn 14 but then the Mercedes driver came back at his rival on the brakes and there was light contact between the two cars.

title: Lindblad's Vegas Qualifying 'such a mess' despite P5 start
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad believes his Qualifying performance for the Las Vegas Grand Prix "was such a mess", despite the Racing Bulls driver set to start from fifth on the grid.

It was a good day for the Faenza outfit as Lindblad not only led the midfield battle but also outpaced one McLaren and both Ferraris, with the Formula 1 rookie gaining a further position as Kimi Antonelli serves a grid penalty.

Having not experienced the track until Thursday’s rain-affected running, Lindblad breezed through the three Qualifying sessions in P7, P6 and P6 while still learning by the lap.

“It's been a tricky day. Basically no laps yesterday, and on any street circuit, any limited running is always more of a challenge," he said.

"So I was having to build a lot throughout today, every lap trying to get more comfortable. Even during Qualifying, I was learning a lot with every lap. So happy with how I learned, how I built.

“[But] it was such a mess. The tyres weren't working, so I had a lot of understeer, I made a bit of a mistake in Turn 8. So it wasn't a perfect lap.

"Also, at the same time, there's a lot that's not gone my way the recent races that's been out of my control, and there's been times I have done very good laps, but due to things you haven't seen it. So I'll take the bit of luck."

Racing Bulls team mate Liam Lawson backed up his team mate with a solid P8 performance after rueing a loss of straight line speed on his final run.

Still it was a double Q3 appearance for the team who are looking to secure fifth in the Teams' standings, and that P8 grid slot will turn to P7 for the race as New Zealander will be promoted following Oscar Piastri's penalty.

"We had a very good car, very good corner speed today,” said the Kiwi.

“Just had no straight line speed, which here is just impossible. I don't really know why, I need to check whether it's something I did on battery usage, or I don't know.

“Honestly, there's not really much you can do. So I'll go and check. But yeah, it's a shame because I think the car was very, very good, and I feel like we did a good job today, and extracted everything out of it.”

title: What the teams said – Qualifying in Las Vegas
excerpt:
Mercedes

Russell topped FP3 and went into Qualifying as the favourite for pole. He was quick in Q1 and Q2 as well, while Antonelli only just scraped into the final segment in P10. But come Q3, Mercedes saw an about turn. Russell wanted a tow and was not happy with being sent out in free air, while Antonelli dropped back and let the whole field pass him.

Somehow, the Italian managed to sneak across the line with a second to go, and despite being tucked up in traffic, he put in a superb lap to grab the fastest time. But it was not pole for the World Champion due to his five-place grid penalty. Russell qualified third, but starts second after his team mate’s grid drop.

Kimi Antonelli, 1st, 1:33.893

"It was certainly a strange qualifying session! I struggled to get the tyres into the right window and didn’t have the feeling with the car that I wanted, so I honestly didn’t expect to end up fastest. On the final lap, several cars pushed past me so I had to back off and create some space to prepare the tyres. The communication with Bono was really good as we were incredibly tight on time, and I crossed the line with only around a second to spare. I then started the lap much closer to the car ahead than you would normally want, which made the corners difficult, but the tow was incredibly powerful on the straights and ultimately helped us get the fastest time. It was high-risk, but it worked out, so I’m happy with the result even if I wasn’t completely happy with my own performance.

"Of course, the grid penalty means we will start P6 tomorrow, but I felt more comfortable with the car on the long runs in FP3 than I did over a single lap. The tow is so strong here that I expect the field to stay close, so we will need to be smart with our overtaking and strategy. We have a good race car underneath us and the target is to fight our way forward and see if we can challenge for the win."

George Russell, 3rd, 1:34.224

"Overall, I’m pleased with how qualifying went. I’ve felt competitive on every lap this weekend and I feel like I’ve got the car beneath me. Of course, I would have loved to take pole, but I don’t think any of us anticipated just how powerful the slipstream would be. Everyone was looking for a tow in Q3 and nobody wanted to be at the front of the pack. Getting it right was very high-risk, though, as you had to leave it incredibly late to get the maximum benefit.

"Starting on the front row for the third race in a row is still a strong position to be in. With the tow being so powerful here, I think it will be difficult for anyone at the front to break away tomorrow. We saw something similar in Monza, so I expect a close and strategic race between several cars at the front. We’ve got good pace and we’re definitely in a position to fight for the win."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"That was an incredibly tight and unpredictable qualifying session. Kimi found a huge tow on his final lap and, although we thought he was far too close to the car ahead, somehow, he made it work to set the fastest time. George looked in a very strong position too; he had what seemed like the ideal gap and had been quickest throughout, but lost some time around Turns 7, 8 and 9. That was unfortunate but he will start on the front-row tomorrow so has every chance of fighting for victory this weekend.

"It should be an entertaining race and, even with Kimi starting P6 after his grid penalty, both cars can hopefully be fighting to be on the podium. With the cars at the front so closely matched, the opening corners could be thrilling to watch. That said, it will be a long race so hopefully we can get through the first lap cleanly and then put ourselves in the mix for the rest of the evening."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We made the most of the learning opportunities in FP3, given it was our only chance to run on a dry track ahead of qualifying. After struggling in the wet yesterday, we were hoping to find the car in a better place today. The early laps of the long run looked sensible and, after a few small tweaks, the balance was reasonable. Our single lap potential also looked good, although some of our competitors didn’t get clean runs, so we expected qualifying to be very close.

"It ended up being quite a messy session for us. We underestimated the advantage of having a tow, but with nobody wanting to be at the front of the pack, positioning the cars with traffic ahead was far from straightforward. George ended up with a reasonable gap for his final effort, while Kimi was at risk of missing the flag and had to start his lap just 1.4 seconds behind Lindblad. We thought that proximity had cost him any chance of improving, so we were both pleased and a little surprised when he managed to go fastest.

"Kimi’s Power Unit penalty drops him back to P6, but with George starting P2, we should be well placed to fight at the front tomorrow. Overtaking looks possible with the long straights and relatively low levels of tyre overheating, so it should make for an interesting race."

title: Alpine left disappointed despite Gasly’s ‘perfect’ Q2 lap
excerpt:
A Las Vegas GP Qualifying session that briefly promised much more ended in disappointment for Alpine as Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto finished at the bottom of Q3 in P9 and P10.

Having been second fastest on intermediates in Thursday’s FP2 session, Gasly again popped up in P2 after a superb lap in Q2.

Given that he took pole at Monza on a track also dominated by long straights, it looked like he might once again at least mix it with the cars from the established frontrunning teams.

However, in what was a messy Q3 session that saw several drivers tripping over each other ahead of the final runs, he wasn’t able to repeat that form, and he had to settle for P9.

“I think Q2 was pretty much the perfect track position, out lap, prep lap, and the way everything sort of worked out,” said the Frenchman. “Tried to do the same in Q3, and unfortunately, it didn't quite work out the same way.

“I think in that first run, there were definitely a few things we could have managed better as a team. But yeah, I think we'll review it all to get stronger and work well. In that second run, it was just a bit, I would say, unlucky, and all these cars bunched up. I had to slow down, open the gap, cold tyres into Turn 1.

“I lost two or three tenths into the first sector, and that was... I feel like at least a position was on the table. I lost by a hundredth to Lawson. So that was clearly at least one position more to get.”

Gasly was sure that he could have finished further up the order, even if a Monza repeat was never on the cards.

“It did feel like everything kind of worked out perfectly [in Q2],” he said. “And I was hoping we at least can get the same, which I think would have put us with Hadjar, like P6 or something like that, in front of Lindblad.

“But honestly, the tow was insane. If you look at the last sector of Antonelli, you just understand how powerful. I've never, ever felt that in a car. So yeah, there was a lot down to that. Unfortunately, it just didn't quite work as we wanted.”

Colapinto, meanwhile, was an encouraging P7 in Q2 but, like Gasly, he also had a difficult final session and thus had to settle for P10.

“I think we are all very disappointed,” he admitted. “The last run was a mess. The previous one, I just took a bit of a feel. I was fully alone on track. So in the straights, I was very slow. But I think the pace was generally there. We had a few places where we could do better and we could improve.

“But the session was just very up and down. Like, some laps you had grip, some laps not. And then the last lap, with all the mess in the prep lap, having a bit of a, of a race together, was not good. So the tyres were not in a good place.

“The lap was nowhere in terms of sector one: no grip, sliding everywhere, tyres very far out the window. And that here matters a lot when you don't do things correctly because of traffic or positioning. You pay it really hard later on in the lap.”

Like Gasly, he stressed the value of the tow: “You probably lose around eight/nine tenths in the straights only with no tows. It's big, and that means in the race it's going to be fun because it's going to create some moves.

“But in quali, it's tricky because you want to be behind someone, but you want also a good prep lap. And if people in front are not doing what you want, then it becomes a real mess.

“It was a pity because I think no run was maximised, so then you always have this feeling that could have been a lot better. But it is what it is – we have to focus on tomorrow.”

title: Russell stunned by 'insane’ tow power in Las Vegas
excerpt:
George Russell has admitted that he was surprised by the “insane” tow power in Qualifying at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Mercedes racer set to start from the front row for Saturday’s race despite not benefitting from a slipstream as others did.

After topping the timesheets earlier on in the weekend’s third and final practice hour, Russell again looked to have good pace in Qualifying.

However, the Briton emerged on track in front of team mate Kimi Antonelli – who was set to serve a five-place grid penalty – during the first runs of Q3, meaning that he could not get a tow from the other Silver Arrows machine.

While he asked over the radio if he could go behind Antonelli, given the World Champion’s impending penalty, the squad ultimately did not use a tow – with Antonelli dropping back during the final runs and only just making the flag to start his lap, one that ultimately put him in P1 before his grid drop demoted him to P6.

Russell, meanwhile, went third fastest behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, meaning that he will start from P2 behind the Dutchman in Saturday’s race.

“It was a very strong session on the whole, but of course it came down to that slipstream and I don't think any of us anticipated how powerful it would be,” Russell reflected after Qualifying.

“It was insane. I still can't wrap my head around it. Kimi said he gained over one second to himself from the lap before, just in the straights.

"But it's high risk – if he started his lap just a few seconds later, he would have had no lap at all, so in the end I'm pleased with the session as a whole.”

Looking ahead to race day, the 28-year-old believes that a number of drivers could be in the fight for victory.

“I think it's going to be very close out there tomorrow,” Russell explained. “As I said, with the slipstream being so powerful, I think it's going to very challenging for the lead car, whoever it may be, to get away, so I think any drivers in the top five or six will be in contention.”

title: Max Verstappen clash with George Russell triggers F1 fan disagreement with stewards
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was handed a warning for the near-miss with George Russel in FP3 at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, but F1 fans see things differently.

F1 fans have taken a different view from the Las Vegas Grand Prix stewards over who was at fault when Max Verstappen and George Russell made contact in final practice.

Verstappen was the driver under investigation after the pair touched at Turn 14. The Red Bull driver was ahead on the approach to the corner when he braked earlier than expected and changed direction under braking.

Russell moved left and tried to pass on the inside. The Mercedes driver had his front axle ahead of Verstappen’s mirror before the two cars made contact.

At the hearing, both drivers discussed the informal agreements that govern how they prepare for a flying lap. The stewards gave those agreements little weight.

What mattered to them was how the two cars had moved and where Russell was in relation to Verstappen.

After reviewing footage, telemetry and team radio, the stewards described Verstappen’s change of direction as "unpredictable" and issued him with a warning for erratic driving.

title: Oscar Piastri reveals jaw-dropping Kimi Antonelli advantage: 'Perfect example'
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has revealed a jaw-dropping gap to pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli in Las Vegas qualifying, explaining that securing a slipstream mattered more than finding the perfect tyre warm-up lap, with Ferrari's failure being the "perfect example".

Antonelli took pole position for Mercedes with a 1:33.893, with Max Verstappen and George Russell completing the top three.

Piastri's best effort of 1:34.899 left him over a second off Antonelli's benchmark, with Lando Norris splitting the pair in fourth for McLaren. Due to a 10-place grid penalty, Piastri will start from 17th.

The timing gaps reflected a qualifying hour dominated by slipstream management on the Strip's long straights, where lining up behind a rival car proved far more valuable than any gains found through tyre preparation.

Piastri said his final runs were compromised by the search for traffic rather than outright pace.

"After Q2, I was pretty happy with how it went, and then Q3 was just a bit messy for a few reasons. Trying to get the right slipstream, you might as well not even go out if you don't get that right," Piastri told select media, including RacingNews365.

"And I mean, even opening the lap here, I think there's a bit of a difference between cars with how much energy they use to Turn 1, and if that's half a second, that can be the difference of three or four tenths down the straight later in the lap, so it's difficult to get right, and I think there were a few things that we probably will review and see if we can do a slightly better job. But I think also my laps were a little bit messy as well."

Ferrari proof all teams were vulnerable

Piastri went further, arguing that the benefit of a tow dwarfed anything a driver could find through getting their tyres into the right window, pointing to Ferrari's struggles as proof that no team was immune.

"Well, there's no point having the perfect warm-up if you have to go first. I think Ferrari is the perfect example. They didn't get a slipstream or not a big enough slipstream, and they're out in Q2," he said.

"I think honestly, any of the top four teams could have done the same thing if they didn't get a tow. So, it's a massive part of these kind of tracks in these cars, and you kind of just have to make do because maybe you can gain a tenth or two with the perfect corner, but you look at Kimi, he's one second faster than me in the last sector. So yeah, no matter what you gain on the tyres, you're always going to lose it and a lot more."

title: Liam Lawson sleeping better with weight of F1 future off his shoulders
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has said he is getting "more hours of sleep" after Racing Bulls confirmed his F1 future for at least next season.

Lawson was left in the precarious position of having no locked-in seat at the Faenza-based squad until recently, despite being one of the standout drivers of the campaign.

Single-handedly, the New Zealander has amassed enough points (75) to put Racing Bulls fifth in the F1 drivers' standings ahead of Alpine (69), despite having spent three rounds racing for Red Bull in place of Isack Hadjar, who suffered a wrist injury over the summer break.

It will be the Alan Permane-led team's best finish in the championship, better than the sixth place achieved by what was then Toro Rosso in 2019 or 2008, when Sebastian Vettel famously took victory at Monza.

However, despite his strong performances, Lawson was at risk of losing his seat to Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov, who is second in the F2 title fight.

Permane and CEO Peter Bayer ultimately decided Lawson should stay put, with Tsolov taking up the reserve role for both Racing Bulls and the top team in 2027, alongside an extensive testing programme as he prepares for F1, likely the year after.

With his immediate future now secure, Lawson was asked if it is a weight off his shoulders and if he was feeling less stressed.

"Yeah, it's definitely a different feeling coming into this weekend [in Las Vegas]," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365.

"Maybe a little bit of weight off, but I feel like... Honestly, the last few races, I've felt pretty good overall."

The delay in snapping up Lawson's signature had become one of the most widely questioned situations in the paddock, given the strength of his results and performances.

Whilst his place in F1 is safe for next year, he may face a repeat scenario in 12 months' time. But for now, he is enjoying the ability to rest more easily.

"Like I've said before, nothing has changed too much," the 24-year-old added. "At least the approach to driving the car hasn't changed. Maybe just a few more hours of sleep, which is nicer."

title: Aston Martin take blame as Lance Stroll flirts with unfortunate F1 record
excerpt:
Aston Martin have taken responsibility for the reliability problems that have left Lance Stroll one retirement away from equalling the F1 record for the most in a single season.

Stroll has retired from 13 grands prix this year. Andrea de Cesaris retired 14 times for Minardi in 1986 and again for Brabham in 1987. Rubens Barrichello matched him with Stewart in 1997.

Two more retirements across Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi would give Stroll the record outright.

Asked about the record ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Stroll pointed to the engine problems Aston Martin and new power unit partner Honda have faced this season.

Aston Martin’s chief trackside officer Mike Krack singled out the battery issues on the Canadian's car.

"That's a point where we have to look in the mirror. We don't have to look at Lance there," Krack told media, including RacingNews365.

"We have to look in the mirror and say, 'We have not done a good enough job to provide a car that is reliable'.

"On his car, there have been most battery issues so far, and that is something that the driver cannot do anything about.

"Unfortunately, he's being named with that stat, which is not at his fault at all. So it's a shame, and it shows that we have to do a better job."

Stroll starts P21 in Las Vegas, where he qualified P20 but received a grid penalty for Aston Martin fitting his ninth energy store (battery) of the season and changing his control electronics. Each driver is allowed three energy stores across the campaign.

title: George Russell teases Las Vegas fight after 'pretty crazy' qualifying
excerpt:
George Russell has teased that it is "all to play for" in the Las Vegas Grand Prix following a "pretty crazy" qualifying.

The Briton qualified in third but will start on the front row alongside Max Verstappen, due to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli claiming pole but having a five-place grid penalty.

Russell has shown strong pace across the weekend at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit and was a contender for pole under the lights.

During qualifying, the Mercedes driver became frustrated by a lack of tow before receiving one on his final lap in Q3.

It was good enough for P3 in the session and left him feeling happier than his Mexico City pole, given how challenging the session was with timings.

"Overall it has been a very solid session and a solid day," said Russell.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance today than I was, let's say, in Mexico a couple of weeks ago when I was on the front row.

"But just timing that out lap, getting the slipstream, was just huge. It was pretty crazy, very similar to what we saw in Monza.

"Obviously Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out pretty well being so close, but it worked out very well for him. But starting P2 with his penalty, it's all to play for."

title: Charles Leclerc admits major Ferrari oversight due to 'weakness' and miscalculation
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has admitted Ferrari did not even discuss him and Lewis Hamilton working together strategically in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The tow was extremely powerful down The Strip in Sin City, but, according to Leclerc, the Scuderia falsely believed tyre temperatures would be "everything" in the grid-setting session.

The Monegasque driver was knocked out alongside his team-mate in Q2 at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, but will line up P10 and P11, respectively, after Oscar Piastri's power unit grid penalty.

Leclerc was unable to get a clean lap in during the second part of qualifying and missed the chance to set a final timed run after being the first driver to take the chequered flag in the dying moments of the segment.

Hamilton, on the other hand, simply did not have the pace or grip needed from his SF-26. The seven-time F1 drivers' champion never looked comfortable, and his elimination was less of a surprise.

However, things may have been different if Ferrari and its drivers, who have endured a tense partnership of late, had been more tactical.

It was put to Leclerc how valuable the slipstream effect was, but due to the difficulties the Italian team has with tyre management, it was not even considered.

"That was not discussed... we thought that tyres were just everything," he told media, including RacingNews365.

"So keeping the temperature in the tyres was the most important thing for us.

"We know it's our weakness. We've got to push. Even in the cool-down laps, we've got to push to keep the tyres [at a] high [temperature].

"I don't know if the others are facing the same issues as we do, but when you have that problem, then it's very difficult to wait for the two cars and to time it well, because that requires you to go slower than you can, and it's very, very tricky for us to keep the tyres and temperatures."

title: Max Verstappen remains tight-lipped over growing Red Bull problem
excerpt:
Max Verstappen will start Saturday's Las Vegas Grand Prix from pole position, but the Red Bull driver remains cagey about a steering problem affecting his RB22.

Verstappen crossed the line second in qualifying but is promoted to pole after a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli.

The four-time champion's second day of track action was not entirely smooth, however, with the Dutchman again reporting trouble with his car, just as he did in Brazil last time out.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, Verstappen played down suggestions of a balance issue, but admitted something is amiss that cannot be fixed for now.

"There's no balance problem," Verstappen said.

"There's just something wrong with the car, but we can't solve that right now. We know where it's coming from.

"This is already the second weekend it's been like this, but I can't say too much about it. It's suddenly become the Brazil problem, that I had that."

The Red Bull driver denied the issue is linked to tyre degradation.

"No, no. It's something completely different, just not how I want it to be," insisted Verstappen. "I can't make much more of it. Otherwise I'm going to start explaining things I don't want to explain."

Isack Hadjar not suffering Max Verstappen problem

According to Verstappen, the problem appears confined to his side of the garage, with team-mate Isack Hadjar unaffected.

"Apparently only on my side of the garage," revealed Verstappen. "I don't know. It's going to be a tough race anyway with the tyre temperature and keeping them in one piece. Mercedes is also very fast, so that'll be a fight."

Asked whether the issue had struck suddenly during the race in Brazil, Verstappen explained it had been there from the start of that weekend.

"I had problems the whole weekend in Brazil," he said. "I'm doing my best [to work around it, ed.], but it's not nice. In certain places I can attack the corners less. It's everywhere; doesn't matter what kind of corner. Then you have to try to adapt, but it's not easy."

Verstappen conceded he has been able to put it aside for qualifying, even if the underlying issue persists.

"I did that in qualifying. We just need to try and fix it. It's gone well for a long time. Just not in Brazil, and not here either. It's not dangerous, but it's not nice," Verstappen concluded.

title: Endless war between Max Verstappen and George Russell enters new chapter
excerpt:
History has a funny tendency to repeat itself, and F1 is no different. That is true of the fractious relationship between Max Verstappen and George Russell, which has entered a new chapter.

Max Verstappen and George Russell crossed paths once more during the third free practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Verstappen overtook his rival just before he was about to start a push lap. Russell was not happy about this, dove back into the slipstream, and tried to force the Dutchman to brake hard heading into Turn 14.

The Red Bull driver, for his part, changed his line while braking, after which the Mercedes pushed the RB22 wide.

The FIA issued Verstappen an official warning for the incident, but most of the attention in the aftermath focused on Russell's reaction.

This incident is not an isolated one. It is now the fourth time that relations between the two drivers have come under significant strain.

Previous confrontations in Azerbaijan 2023, Qatar 2024, and Spain 2025 had already caused considerable tension. Las Vegas now adds a new chapter to that story.

Speaking to Sky Sports F1, Russell made clear what he thought of Verstappen’s move. According to the Briton, while the rules do allow you to pass someone who is just about to start a fast lap, that doesn’t mean such a move is sportsmanlike.

"I think a warning was fine," he said. "But there's nothing in the rules to say you can't overtake someone who is starting a lap.

"When you do this, you are screwing this person over. He does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it.

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

The remarks are reminiscent of previous confrontations between the two. The trigger varies each time, but their mutual irritations have become a recurring theme.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

Bully Verstappen and underdog Russell

Relations began to seriously deteriorate during the sprint race in Azerbaijan in 2023. Russell and Verstappen battled side by side through the first three turns, after which Russell's Mercedes understeered and hit the Red Bull's sidepod.

The RB19 sustained damage to its floor and sidepod in the incident. Verstappen immediately sought out Russell in parc fermé afterwards.

"Man, none of us have any grip. We all need to leave a little space. But expect the same next time, asshole," Verstappen told him at the time. The stewards considered it a standard racing incident and did not intervene.

In Qatar 2024, tensions escalated further. Verstappen received a grid penalty and a penalty point after driving too slowly during the cool-down lap in Q3, forcing Russell to swerve out of the way.

Verstappen was particularly furious about the way Russell had pressed the stewards for a penalty.

"I have a lot of respect for drivers, but after last night, I’ve completely lost that respect for him. I just thought it was ridiculous how he tried to force a penalty down my throat," Verstappen said at the time.

Russell went even further in Abu Dhabi. He called Verstappen a "bully" and claimed that the Dutchman had threatened to deliberately run him off the track. Verstappen has always denied that accusation.

[Article continues below]

That moment in Barcelona

Last season, too, the relationship between the two drivers remained strained. In Canada, Russell accused Verstappen of overtaking behind the safety car, after he himself had braked conspicuously to force the Dutchman into an overtaking manoeuvre. Red Bull filed a protest in response, but it was rejected.

Two weeks earlier, another confrontation had already taken place in Spain. After letting the Brit pass, he deliberately ran his RB21 into the side of Russell’s Mercedes. The Dutchman received a ten-second time penalty and three penalty points.

At the time, Russell called it a deliberate move. Verstappen later acknowledged that he had made a mistake. "The only point of criticism is the situation in Barcelona. What happened there wasn’t great, of course, but it was also because I care a lot."

The incident in Las Vegas has added yet another chapter to the now-long-standing friction between the two. Afterwards, Russell left little doubt that he no longer intends to simply accept Verstappen’s actions.

title: Fernando Alonso addresses potential Honda safety concern in Las Vegas
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has addressed the possibility of safety concerns for other F1 drivers in the Las Vegas Grand Prix, given the straight-line speed deficit his car is facing.

Alonso qualified 19th on the road in Nevada but will start 18th after Carlos Sainz's engine change penalty, but the Aston Martin machines are struggling for speed on the long Vegas straights - a common problem all season with the Honda power unit.

Alonso was 2.736s slower in Q1 than segment topper George Russell, with the two-time champion estimating that around 2.5s of this came on the long straights, including on the Strip and from the last corner to the final left high-speed kink, as he pointed out.

"Exactly as expected," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365, when asked how complicated the session was.

"Monza and Vegas are the worst tracks for us with the longest straights.

"So, yeah, we lost like 2.5 seconds or three seconds on the straights, and in the corners, we were quite competitive.

"I think we were 2.8s from P1 in Q1, and I think we lose more or less that on the straights."

Alonso was then asked if he had any safety concerns regarding the lack of straight-line speed.

"Yeah, but I think the other teams know that when they are behind the Honda engine, they [need to] take extra metres."

Then, when asked for his take on the experience of Las Vegas, Alonso declared that "it is nice, but we don't have the same cars, so it is not really a competition or race. It is demo laps for us."

[Article continues below]

Alonso on the Vegas event

Alonso also voiced his displeasure at the scheduling of Las Vegas in the schedule, forming the first leg of a triple header with Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and coming off the back of a trip back to Europe after a triple header in the United States, Mexico City, and Sao Paulo.

"It is quite far away from Europe, and we've been in Austin and Mexico two weeks ago, two hours away, and then we went to Brazil, and then we went to Europe," he said.

"We come back here for 72 hours, and then we go to Europe because we race in Qatar, so it doesn't make sense to have the race this weekend."

title: Max Verstappen issues blunt two-word response after George Russell collision
excerpt:
Max Verstappen responded with just two words, "Nothing happened," when asked whether he was unhappy with how George Russell had handled their clash during FP3 in Las Vegas.

The pair made contact approaching the 90-degree left-hander at Turn 14 late in the session, with Verstappen overtaking Russell on the straight before braking early and moving unpredictably as the Mercedes driver dived down the inside to reclaim track position.

The incident did not trigger a flag and neither car suffered terminal damage, allowing both drivers to complete the session without further disruption.

But the FIA stewards summoned both men afterwards and handed Verstappen an official warning for changing direction under braking, ruling that his driving fell below the expected standard, even if it did not merit a grid penalty.

Russell was far less willing to let the moment pass. The Briton has publicly accused Verstappen of repeatedly disrupting rivals on track and called on the field to stop tolerating his conduct, reviving tension between the two that dates back to their bitter dispute following the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix qualifying penalty.

Speaking to select media including RacingNews365, Russell left no doubt about his view of the clash.

"No confusion. I mean, it was pretty clear, I think."

Verstappen, speaking to the same media, offered little else by way of explanation, sticking to his brief dismissal of the incident.

With Verstappen and Russell locked in a direct fight for second place in the drivers' championship with three rounds left, the Red Bull driver's refusal to engage further leaves Russell's frustration unanswered heading into qualifying in Las Vegas.

title: McLaren explain how a plastic bag derailed surprising Lando Norris attack
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has detailed how a plastic bag wrecked Lando Norris's surprising bid for pole position at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Norris qualified fourth on the road for round 21 of the season, but will be promoted to third after qualifying winner Kimi Antonelli lost his pole position due to the five-place grid drop he was already carrying for a new ICE.

Max Verstappen and George Russell are therefore promoted to the front-row, with Norris 0.093s behind Verstappen and 0.020s slower than Russell on a track not expected to suit McLaren's MCL40 machine.

The car is known to be draggy, with McLaren opting for shorter gear ratios than other front-running teams, meaning the car lacks top-end straight-line speed.

However, with the aid of the slipstream from other cars, Norris was able to produce a lap-time which has put him at the sharp end of the grid, and in the prime position to take over the lead should anything befall Verstappen and Russell on the opening lap after their feud restarted in FP3.

In his media briefing at the end of the day, team principal Stella revealed how a plastic bag had got stuck in Norris's floor in the session, potentially costing a tenth of a second in performance - about the margin Norris was behind Verstappen, who inherited pole.

During the second free practice session on Thursday, a brief red flag was flown after a plastic wrap made its way onto the track, which was then run over by Aston Martin's Lance Stroll, with other small debris, such as crisp packets, also blowing on the racing surface - which is opened to the public after the cessation of track activities.

"If anything, we could have been even more competitive in qualifying, especially on Lando's side," Stella began to media, including RacingNews365.

"He was quite unlucky because a plastic bag got stuck in the floor and we lost quite a lot of downforce.

"So considering that one-tenth of a second would make a big difference, and there certainly was a tenth of a second in a plastic bag, which is a bit of a shame.

"But we need to look at how we keep the car raceable in the race.

"If we look at Monza, we saw that with the towing effect you can actually stay tangled and linked to the other cars.

"So we are definitely looking forward [to the race] and are encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive."

[Article continues below]

McLaren' straight-line speed problems

Turning to the straight-line speed woes the team has had in 2026, Stella praised the efforts to ensure Norris and Oscar Piastri were placed in the queue of cars accordingly to enable them to have the best access to the powerful tow.

"We definitely had some concerns in terms of how suitable the demands of this circuit would be for the car at high speed," he added.

"It is not only the top speed, but it is also the top speed that combines with the tow, so you go into operating regimes of the engine that, with our ratios, are not ideal.

"We know that the drag, from an aerodynamic point of view, is not a point of trend, but we discuss in the debrief that we need to look holistically at all the conditions that influence the top speed.

"But certainly, we have seen here traits that are similar to Monza and Baku, and in all conditions, we were not particularly competitive.

"I think what we have done better here is to mitigate this by having really good positioning in qualifying. The car was pretty much where we wanted it to be in qualifying, and this definitely helped because I have to say that it seems like, with these regulations, the drag reduction when you follow one car or even multiple cars is more than in the past, and therefore there's an even higher incentive to be positioned in the right place."

title: Exclusive: Oliver Bearman exploring shock move to F1 rival as Haas contract delay rumbles on
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman could be on the brink of a remarkable end to the F1 season, which would see him leave Haas, sever ties with Ferrari, and potentially join a Formula 1 rival, RacingNews365 understands.

Bearman is the last remaining driver on the F1 grid yet to be confirmed for next season. The Briton and Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu have expressed confidence over the past few weeks that the matter would be resolved and the partnership would continue.

However, according to sources, Bearman remains in limbo as he and his management have long expected the 21-year-old to race for Ferrari next year following two highly successful seasons at Haas where he has enjoyed exemplary treatment over that time, notably with unswerving support from team principal Komatsu.

The path to hoped-for promotion, however, is naturally blocked by Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton. The seven-time F1 champion revealed in his media session on Wednesday ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix that he is only “halfway” through his contract and that he has every intention of seeing it through.

Bearman's situation is further complicated by the fact he now has another Ferrari Academy driver product, Rafael Camara, as his team-mate after the Brazilian impressed in a recent shootout and was chosen to replace the axed Esteban Ocon.

Bearman’s management, however, is apparently unwilling to take the risk of Camara dealing a blow to their driver, just as Bearman did to Ocon, against all prior expectations, and they are now looking for a way out of his current ties.

That is the real reason a new contract has not been signed until now.

In Las Vegas, in an interview with F1TV, Bearman, who had always previously emphasised that a new deal was imminent, changed tone and gave the impression the situation was out of his hands, and that any new contract could be finalised at any moment.

According to our sources, this new narrative serves multiple purposes: on one hand, it attempts to shift the blame onto other parties in the eyes of the public, and on the other, it paves the way for the move they are hoping for - a split.

[Article continues below]

Where does Bearman go?

In Bearman’s situation, the only acceptable move is to secure a race seat immediately for 2027 somewhere outside Ferrari’s sphere of influence.

The driver’s representatives have explored numerous options since the summer: there have been whispers in the paddock of talks held with Mercedes and McLaren, as well as Aston Martin, at a time when there was a possibility Fernando Alonso could retire at the end of the season. RacingNews365 understands that discussions also took place with Williams.

Now, only one strictly theoretical option remains: Alpine.

The Enstone-based outfit previously indicated that Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto would again form their driver lineup in 2027, but a lot has happened since the Argentine driver’s contract was announced on August 27th.

In the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, a reckless overtaking manoeuvre from Colapinto on Gasly resulted in the retirement of both cars. Although Colapinto regretted the incident, word around the team is that the atmosphere changed after that moment of madness.

Internal morale has also not been helped by the toxic environment created by Colapinto's fanbase on social media, forcing the team into continual explanations.

Sources have indicated that the trust previously placed in Colapinto by Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive advisor and de facto leader, has wavered following the incident with Gasly, allied to his inconsistent performances.

Briatore is renowned as a pragmatic manager who has, on countless occasions throughout his career, proven that no driver's seat is bulletproof and that he does not hesitate to act when a situation demands.

RacingNews365 understands that Bearman’s management is trying to capitalise on this. Multiple meetings have taken place between Bearman’s representatives and Briatore - in the paddock and in Monaco where Bearman and the team leader are living.

As to whether a deal will happen depends on whether complex contractual issues will be resolved, whilst any potential agreement also requires a substantial financial package from the British driver.

Colapinto’s main sponsor, Mercado Libre, reportedly pays Alpine at least $20 million. If the Bearman camp has managed to put together a similar package, Briatore could easily decide to pull the trigger.

With expectations set to rise following the arrival of new title sponsor Gucci next year, industry experts consulted by RacingNews365 believe a Gasly–Bearman pairing would offer completely different optics than the current one.

As for Colapinto, he could remain at Alpine as third driver, a role vacant after Paul Aron recently departed.

It cannot be ruled out that he would move heaven and earth to return to Williams. There has been talk in the paddock of late about an increase in meetings between the driver and team principal James Vowles, who recently answered "yes" in an interview when asked if he could imagine Colapinto returning to the Grove-based team in the future.

The matter is likely to drag on for a while longer, and a final decision may not materialise until the winter break.
